title: Education Gadfly Weekly, Volume 26, Number 36
author: Fordham Institute
source: The Education Gadfly Weekly / Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 10, 2026
summary: This issue of Fordham's weekly digest bundles three of the institute's own commentary pieces — on screen/AI-driven grade inflation, competing state 'portrait of a graduate' policies, and the reliability of homework in the AI era — around a single argument: American high schools have let go of the basic conditions that make learning possible. Each blurb is written by Fordham staff in the outlet's own analytical voice, not just linked, so the digest itself functions as a mini-editorial about attention, rigor, and accountability. The throughline is that new competency- and AI- driven pressures are exposing how thin many schools' standards for honest work have become. It closes with pointers to a full research report and past ICYMI commentary, reinforcing the survey findings with data.
points: Frames screens, AI misuse, and grade inflation as three symptoms of one underlying failure: adults no longer holding students to consistent standards.
Uses Massachusetts vs. New York as a live natural experiment in how 'portrait of a graduate' policies can preserve or abandon rigor.
Treats homework's evidentiary value as newly suspect once AI makes it easy to produce polished work without doing the thinking.
Positions strengthened, harder-to-fake assessment (not banning technology outright) as the actual lever schools have available.
quotes: High school students report widespread screen distraction, AI misuse, and grading practices that make it easier to earn high marks without mastering the relevant material. A new Fordham survey suggests that we will only solve these problems by restoring the basic conditions for learning: attention, effort, honest work, and adults willing to hold adolescents to high expectations.

Portraits of a graduate often trade the rigor and transparency of a traditional diploma for vague competencies. But Massachusetts may be charting a better path. The state's proposal pairs broader demonstrations of aptitude with end-of-course exams, district-level scoring rules, and requirements for helping students plan their lives after high school.

AI is making traditional homework far less reliable as evidence of learning, with new research suggesting that students can use chatbots and other tech to earn better assignment grades while doing, and learning, less. Schools should respond by strengthening assessments and taking a hard look at whether independent homework does more harm than good.

Few topics in K–12 education have garnered more attention in the past year than the use and abuse of technology and screens in schools. Long-simmering tensions about ubiquitous cell phones ran headlong into renewed concerns about school-issued devices and threats of AI-enabled cheating.

His findings show that school-issued devices are often misused, making them nearly as distracting as students' personal cell phones. Combine that with unethical use of AI and rampant grade inflation, and we've seriously hollowed out the American high school experience.
